presentingComplaint: Worsening left-sided headache, fever and confusion for 6 days, with a witnessed generalised seizure and rapid deterioration into shock this morning.
history: Type-2 diabetic tea-estate worker with a 3-month history of a foul-smelling discharging right ear (chronic suppurative otitis media), previously treated with repeated short courses of oral antibiotics. Over the past week he developed a progressively severe, largely right-temporal headache with nausea, low-grade fever and increasing drowsiness. Family noted uncharacteristic irritability and word-finding difficulty over 48h. This morning he had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting ~2 minutes followed by prolonged post-ictal confusion, then became cold, clammy and unrousable, prompting emergency transfer. No recent travel, no IV drug use, no known immunodeficiency other than poorly controlled diabetes (last HbA1c 9.4%).
examination: Toxic, drowsy (GCS E3 V4 M5 = 12), not following commands consistently. Peripherally shut down with cool mottled extremities and prolonged capillary refill (4s). Right ear with mucopurulent discharge and a dull, immobile tympanic membrane; mastoid mildly tender. Neurological: subtle left-sided pronator drift and left facial asymmetry, mild neck stiffness but no photophobia. Fundi without frank papilloedema. Chest clear; abdomen soft. No rash.
imaging: Contrast CT head: 3.4 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe with surrounding vasogenic oedema, mild midline shift (4 mm) and effacement of the ipsilateral temporal horn; opacified right mastoid air cells with bony dehiscence into the middle cranial fossa. MRI brain with DWI: central restricted diffusion (low ADC) within the lesion, confirming pyogenic abscess rather than necrotic tumour.
microbiology: Empiric blood cultures grew a Gram-negative bacillus at 36h. CT-guided/neurosurgical aspiration of the abscess yielded frank pus; Gram stain showed Gram-negative bacilli plus Gram-positive cocci. Cultures (aerobic + anaerobic) grew Proteus mirabilis and Peptostreptococcus spp.; the P. mirabilis was fully susceptible to third-generation cephalosporins (no ESBL). CSF not sampled by LP due to mass effect / herniation risk.
differentialDiagnoses: Pyogenic brain abscess (otogenic, right temporal lobe)
Cerebral neoplasm / metastasis with central necrosis
Acute ischaemic stroke with post-ictal deficit
finalDiagnosis: Otogenic pyogenic brain abscess (right temporal lobe) complicated by septic shock and acute kidney injury; polymicrobial (Proteus mirabilis + anaerobes) secondary to chronic suppurative otitis media / mastoiditis.
citations: Surviving Sepsis Campaign - Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock, 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Brain Abscess
stewardship: Life-threatening intracranial infection with septic shock: after two blood-culture sets, start empiric broad-spectrum IV therapy that penetrates the CNS and covers the likely otogenic polymicrobial flora (streptococci, anaerobes, Enterobacterales) - ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 8-hourly, with vancomycin added to cover possible staphylococci/resistant Gram-positives pending cultures. Concurrent source control (neurosurgical aspiration of the abscess and ENT management of the mastoiditis) is essential and diagnostic. Once aspirate and blood cultures identified fully-cephalosporin-susceptible P. mirabilis with anaerobes and no MRSA/staphylococci, de-escalate by STOPPING vancomycin and continuing ceftriaxone + metronidazole, completing a prolonged (6-8 week) IV course with serial imaging. Bundle: fluid resuscitation, early noradrenaline for MAP >=65, glycaemic control, and renal dosing review as AKI resolves.
contraindications: Lumbar puncture contraindicated given ring-enhancing mass with midline shift (herniation risk)
Avoid nephrotoxic combinations / dose-adjust vancomycin and monitor levels in AKI
Corticosteroids only if significant mass effect/impending herniation, not routine
edgeCases: DWI restricted diffusion distinguishes pyogenic abscess from necrotic tumour when the ring-enhancing lesion is otherwise ambiguous
Repeated prior short antibiotic courses may render blood/CSF cultures sterile, making stereotactic aspiration the key to a microbiological diagnosis and safe de-escalation
Septic shock from an intracranial focus is uncommon; a concurrent otogenic bacteraemia/mastoiditis explains the haemodynamic collapse
expectedMaiK: Recognise a ring-enhancing intracranial lesion with septic shock as an otogenic pyogenic brain abscess: resuscitate for shock, secure blood cultures, start empiric CNS-penetrating ceftriaxone + metronidazole (+ vancomycin), obtain urgent neurosurgical aspiration for source control and culture, then de-escalate on results.
